existing_tips: After negation, 'des' becomes 'd'' before a vowel: 'pas d'amis'. The partitive article disappears.
'De l'' is the partitive before vowels: de l'eau, de l'huile, de l'argent. Same meaning as du/de la:
'Avoir mal à' = to have pain in: j'ai mal au dos (my back hurts), j'ai mal aux dents (I have a tooth
'Vieux' has special forms: vieux (m. before consonant), vieil (m. before vowel), vieille (f.), vieux
When inverting with il/elle/on, add '-t-' between two vowels for pronunciation: A-t-il ? Va-t-elle ?
French says 'it makes' for weather: `il fait beau` (the weather's nice), `il fait froid`. Same patte
'Est-ce que' placed before a statement turns it into a yes/no question. It's the most common questio
'Avoir tort' = to be wrong, 'avoir raison' = to be right. French 'has wrong/reason'.
'Lequel/laquelle' = Which one. Agrees with the noun: lequel (m.), laquelle (f.), lesquels (m. pl.),
French negation wraps the verb: `je ne sais pas`. In speech the `ne` often drops (`je sais pas`) but
`on` is the all-purpose informal 'we' in spoken French: `on va au cinéma` = 'we're going to the movi
'Avoir hâte de' = to be eager to / can't wait to. Literally 'to have haste to'.
'Avoir mal à' + body part = to hurt: 'j'ai mal au ventre'. The article contracts: à + le = au.
'De quoi' = What...of/about. Use after verbs that take 'de': avoir besoin de, parler de, avoir envie
`on` also = English 'one' or 'they' (impersonal): `on dit que...` = 'they say that...'. Two meanings
In questions, 'est-ce que nous' sounds natural. The inverted form 'sommes-nous' is more formal.
'Les magasins' – use 'les' for all/general plural nouns. 'Des' would mean 'some' stores.
Reflexive verbs use a pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous/se) before the verb. `Je m'appelle` = 'I call myse
'Être en vacances' = to be on vacation. Note the plural 'vacances' – always plural in French.
After negation, 'du/de la/des' become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. Literally 'to be of agreement'. Very common expression.
'Qu'est-ce que' = what (as object). Literally 'What is it that'. Used for asking about things/action
'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
'Avoir confiance en' = to trust / to have confidence in. Another avoir expression for a feeling.
